newsitem.title: FRANCE: TPS able to compete with Canal -du Bouzet.
newsitem.headline: TPS able to compete with Canal -du Bouzet.

text.p: Digital satellite television service TPS is in a position to compete with CanalSatellite, Canal Plus's satellite unit, Walter Vejdovsky, analyst at broker du Bouzet, said on Thursday.

Speaking to reporters about his study of the media sector of the Paris bourse, he said that TPS, operated by TF1, had taken half the subscribers to digital television services in France since the beginning of this year.
TPS launched last December, while Canal Plus was the first on the digital market with CanalSatellite last April.
"We think that TPS is really able to take a third of the digital television market," Vejdovsky said.
He declined to predict the size of the French digital television market in the medium term.
"The positions are not yet definitive. It is not a war between established positions but a war of jostling for place," he said.
TPS has 116,000 subscribers currently and has said it will have 300,000 by the end of this year, more than its initial projection of 250,000.

TPS managing director Cyrille du Peloux said last week that the service should become profitable once it has a million subscribers, which should happen around the end of 1999 or at the beginning of the year 2000.
CanalSatellite has 500,000 subscribers of whom 300,000 take its digital service.
It expects to have 500,000 digital subscribers at the end of this year and reach operating break-even at the end of 1998 or early in 1999, with 850,000 to 900,000 subscribers.
Vejdovsky said Canal Plus is confronted with the delicate task of converting subscribers who currently only take its encoded channel to its digital service without losing them.
"With TPS, everything is a 100 percent gain. There is no duplication," he said.

TPS has several advantages, particularly its exclusive contract to broadcast the French general channels in digital form by satellite, given that many households cannot receive them via terrestrial means.
TPS also has around a third of the Hollywood studio rights, while Canal Plus, which has another third, has to use its rights on its parent channel, which is broadcast on terrestrial television.
"CanalSatellite's basic service costs the same as that of TPS, but to have Hollywood films you have to subscribe to Canal Plus, which costs you 300 francs a month instead of 130 francs," he said.

TPS could be an example prompting competition to Canal Plus in other countries, he said. In Italy RAI and STET have said they wanted to move into digital television to compete with Telepiu, run by Canal Plus since it merged with NetHold, which owns 45 percent of Telepiu.
In Spain, Canal Plus faces a broadside from a group led by Telefonica and supported by the government.

If Telefonica comes in with Canal Plus's Spanish unit, CanalSatelite Digital, as some observers suggest, Canal Plus would be diluted to around 12 percent of CanalSatelite Digital from about 25 percent currently, he said.
